 El Niño explained: What it means for Kenya’s December rainy season
 Sunday 08th November, 2026 07:42 AM | 
 By Felix Kyalo 
 Flooding caused by El Niño rains. 
 El Niño is back in the global weather conversation, with a warming Pacific Ocean raising questions about rainfall patterns, drought, and the possibility of flooding in different parts of the world, including Kenya.
 But what exactly is El Niño, why does it happen, and how can warming ocean waters thousands of kilometres away influence the weather experienced in Kenya?
 The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) on Sunday, November 8, 2026, explained this in the first episode of its new Weather Talk Kenya programme, featuring Principal Meteorologist Dr. Finas Okoth.
 One of the key points Okoth emphasised is that El Niño should not be confused with rainfall. Rather, it is a climate phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and influences weather patterns across the world.
 “To start with, the El Niño is not rainfall. I’d like to clarify that El Niño is not rainfall. El Niño is a warming which happens so far away in the Pacific,” Okoth explained.
 His clarification is important because El Niño does not automatically mean heavy rainfall everywhere. Its effects vary depending on geographical location, atmospheric conditions and other climate systems.
 What exactly is El Niño?
 El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by the unusual warming of surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. 
 Under normal conditions, winds blowing along the equatorial Pacific push warm surface water towards the western Pacific, around Australia and Indonesia. Cooler water rises towards the surface in the eastern Pacific, near the coast of South America.
 During El Niño, these winds weaken, allowing warmer ocean water to spread towards the central and eastern Pacific.
 This changes the relationship between the ocean and the atmosphere, influencing the movement of air, the formation of clouds and the distribution of rainfall across different parts of the world.
 In simple terms, an increase in ocean temperatures in one part of the world can change where rain falls thousands of kilometres away.
 Okoth explained that the phenomenon occurs periodically, with warming episodes developing at intervals of approximately two to seven years.
 “During certain years, this part of the ocean warms. Like this year in 2026. We had a warming in 2023. We had a warming in 2015. And the most pronounced one is the year 1997, which everyone can remember,” he said.
 The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) on Sunday, November 8, 2026, explained this in the first episode of its new Weather Talk Kenya programme, featuring Principal Meteorologist Dr. Finas Okoth. PHOTO/ @MeteoKenya 
 The 1997–1998 El Niño remains a significant reference point because of the exceptionally heavy rainfall and flooding experienced across parts of East Africa, including Kenya.
 Why El Niño affects some countries differently
 Although El Niño begins in the Pacific Ocean, its influence extends far beyond the region.
 Changes in ocean temperatures affect atmospheric circulation, shifting rainfall patterns and influencing weather conditions in different parts of the world.
 Some countries experience increased rainfall, while others face prolonged dry conditions.
 Okoth cited Australia as an example of a region that experiences drought during certain El Niño episodes.
 He also pointed to Egypt, Sudan, northern South Sudan and Ethiopia, where rainfall can be below normal during the phenomenon.
 These differences explain why El Niño cannot simply be described as a global rainy season.
 The same climate phenomenon can contribute to flooding in one region while increasing the risk of drought in another. 
 Why the warming is significant
 The development of El Niño has become particularly important during the second half of 2026 because it coincides with the October-November-December (OND) rainfall season.
 This is the period when Kenya receives its short rains, making the warming of the Pacific Ocean an important factor in seasonal weather forecasting.
 Okoth said meteorologists had been monitoring changes in Pacific Ocean temperatures and comparing observations with climate models to establish whether the warming had reached the levels associated with El Niño.
 He explained that the thresholds used by meteorologists to identify the phenomenon had been surpassed.
 “The thresholds that we use to trigger… have been surpassed,” he said.
 The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) on Sunday, November 8, 2026, explained this in the first episode of its new Weather Talk Kenya programme, featuring Principal Meteorologist Dr. Finas Okoth. PHOTO/ @MeteoKenya 
 The meteorologist added that observations from the monitored ocean region had confirmed a warming signal, with climate models also being used to project how the phenomenon would develop.
 He explained that meteorologists assess the warming using successive three-month periods, including August-September-October, September-October-November and October-November-December.
 This approach helps establish whether the warming is sustained rather than a temporary increase in ocean temperatures.
 The October-November period is therefore important in determining how the developing climate phenomenon could influence the ongoing OND rainfall season and the months that follow.
 What El Niño means for Kenya
 For Kenya, the main concern is how changes in the Pacific Ocean could influence rainfall during the short-rains season.
 El Niño can favour enhanced rainfall across parts of East Africa, although the amount and distribution of rain vary across the region.
 For Kenyan households, farmers and businesses, changes in rainfall can have direct consequences.
 Increased rainfall can support agricultural production and improve water availability, but excessive rainfall can also cause flooding, damage roads, disrupt transport, destroy crops and displace families.
 However, El Niño alone cannot determine the weather conditions in every county. Other climate systems, including the Indian Ocean Dipole, as well as local geographical conditions, also influence rainfall.
 This makes it important for Kenyans to follow seasonal forecasts and county-specific weather advisories rather than assume that every part of the country will experience similar conditions.
 Through Weather Talk Kenya, the meteorological agency is seeking to make complex weather information easier for the public to understand and use when preparing for changing conditions. 
 As Okoth’s explanation illustrates, understanding El Niño starts with recognising that it is not rainfall itself, but a warming of ocean waters that can influence where rainfall occurs across the world.
